primitives.name: Aphasic Sensory Guidance
primitives.verbatim_quote: The modern mode of teaching deaf mutes to articulate consists in making them attentive to certain laryngeal, labial, thoracic, and other sensations, the reproduction of which becomes a guide to their vocalization.
primitives.assumptions: Speech production depends on internal sensory feedback; external auditory cues are replaced by tactile/kinesthetic ones.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When L,B,T → 0, V becomes uncontrolled or absent.

layer2.mapping: GSE maps sensory modalities to vocal output; GSI models how sensory substitution enables linguistic behavior.
layer2.telemetry: Accuracy of articulation in deaf individuals trained via tactile feedback.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that volition is not pure intention but grounded in sensory feedback. The sensory feedback control primitive establishes that motor acts require real-time sensory validation—when this is removed (as in anesthesia), motor precision collapses. Volitional conceptualization builds upon this by asserting that even in the absence of external sensory input, the mind must internally reconstruct sensory models to form intentions. This suggests a dual-layered architecture: one where sensory feedback drives immediate action, and another where memory-based sensory models support abstract intentionality. Aphasic sensory guidance extends this by showing that even in the absence of hearing, tactile and kinesthetic feedback can substitute for auditory guidance in speech. These primitives form a coherent framework for understanding how sensory experience underpins both immediate action and higher-order volition. The failure modes are clear: loss of sensory input leads to stochastic or absent action, while loss of internal sensory models leads to volitional paralysis. The mathematical structure is one of conditional dependency: action depends on sensory feedback, and intention depends on internalized sensory models.
